strengths: The paper targets spatial acceleration for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), an important and underexplored direction compared to temporal pruning and caching techniques.
The identification and decomposition of spatial upsampling failure modes into aliasing artifacts (edge bleeding) and noise-timestep mismatch artifacts are insightful and well-illustrated.

The proposed Noise-Timestep Rescheduling with Distribution Matching (NT-DM) provides a principled mathematical framework for adapting correlated noise injection to training-free flow matching by minimizing the Jensen-Shannon Divergence against the target non-uniform timestep schedule.

Extensive experimental validation across FLUX.1-dev and SD3 shows that RALU substantially outperforms existing spatial and temporal baselines (e.g., Bottleneck Sampling, ToCa, RAS), retaining high visual quality and prompt fidelity at up to 7x speedup.
The method demonstrates clear orthogonality and compatibility with temporal caching techniques, yielding compound speedup benefits.
weaknesses: In Stage 2, performing Tweedie estimation followed by a full VAE decoding pass to run Canny edge detection adds pipeline complexity. Although the authors show the theoretical FLOPs are small (<1%), running the VAE decoder mid-generation incurs memory fragmentation and runtime overhead compared to estimating token saliency directly from latent features or cross-/self-attention maps.

The scheduling parameters (such as the number of steps per stage $N_k$ and transition boundaries $e_k$) are heuristically pre-selected before running the numerical optimization for $h_k$ and $c$, which requires per-speedup configuration tuning.

The evaluation would be strengthened by comparing against or discussing other token reduction techniques for DiTs, such as token merging/pruning methods (e.g., ToMe/ToCa variants and attention-compression baselines), rather than primarily comparing against a single training-free spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling).

strengths: Addresses an important and less explored direction in Diffusion Transformer (DiT) acceleration: spatial-domain acceleration as opposed to standard temporal layer/token caching.

Provides a sound theoretical and mathematical grounding for rectified flow models; the derivation of correlated noise injection and the Noise-Timestep rescheduling via Distribution Matching (NT-DM) systematically mitigate covariance and timestep distribution shifts.

Strong empirical efficiency gains: achieves up to 7x speedup on FLUX.1-dev and 3x on Stable Diffusion 3, preserving image quality (FID, CLIP-IQA) and text-image alignment metrics significantly better than existing spatial (Bottleneck Sampling) and temporal (ToCa, RAS) baselines.
Demonstrates clear orthogonality and complementarity with existing temporal acceleration methods, showing further speedup gains when combined with token caching.
Extensive qualitative analysis, including zoom-in comparisons across multiple baselines and extensive uncurated visual samples in the appendix.
weaknesses: The operational details of the mixed-resolution attention mechanism in Stage 2 are insufficiently detailed; the paper does not clearly specify how positional embeddings are adjusted or how tokens of differing spatial granularities are packed and processed efficiently without incurring engineering overheads in optimized attention kernels.

Relying on Tweedie's approximation followed by full VAE decoding and Canny edge detection introduces pipeline complexity; although VAE FLOPs are minimal, memory traffic, synchronization, and edge filtering operations may introduce non-trivial wall-clock latency overheads that are not individually benchmarked.

Hyperparameter selection involves several hand-tuned settings (stage boundaries e_k, step allocations N, and the top-k selection ratio), and the robustness of the JSD optimization across diverse aspect ratios or arbitrary resolutions warrants further empirical validation.

The formulation of NT-DM is tightly coupled to rectified flow matching formulations, limiting direct plug-and-play applicability to standard DDPM/DDIM-based diffusion backbones without additional theoretical extensions.

strengths: Principled and novel formulation for training-free spatial acceleration: While inference acceleration for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) has mostly concentrated on temporal caching or model pruning, spatial acceleration has remained underexplored. The paper clearly identifies and categorizes the two primary failure modes of latent upsampling—edge aliasing and noise-timestep distribution mismatch—and offers targeted solutions for both.

Sound mathematical derivation for flow matching trajectory correction: The theoretical derivation of the correlated noise injection parameters (a, b, and rescheduled timestep s_{k+1}) to project upsampled latents back onto the rectified flow trajectory (Eq. 5-6, Appendix A.1) is mathematically sound. Formulating timestep rescheduling via JSD minimization against the base model's non-uniform timestep distribution (NT-DM) provides a principled alternative to heuristic schedule alterations.

Strong empirical speedups with minimal degradation: On modern large-scale DiTs (FLUX.1-dev and SD3), RALU demonstrates convincing quantitative and qualitative results, achieving up to ~7.0x speedup on FLUX and ~3.0x on SD3. It consistently outperforms baselines such as Bottleneck Sampling, ToCa, and RAS across FID, NIQE, CLIP-IQA, and alignment metrics (GenEval, T2I-CompBench).

Orthogonality to temporal acceleration: The authors demonstrate that RALU is complementary to feature caching methods (e.g., boosting FLUX speedup from 7.02x to 7.94x with minor metric variation), showcasing its utility as an independent acceleration axis.

Thorough visual and uncurated qualitative evidence: The paper includes clear diagnostic figures illustrating artifact emergence (Figs. 2, 4, S1) alongside extensive uncurated generations across CC12M prompts (Figs. S8-S11).
weaknesses: Overhead and practicality of intermediate pixel-space decoding: In Stage 2, estimating x_0 via Tweedie's formula and decoding it to pixel space via the VAE decoder to run Canny edge detection introduces GPU kernel synchronization and memory footprint overheads. Although the theoretical FLOP count is low (<1%), running full VAE decoding mid-generation can create hardware bottlenecks, particularly under batched inference or memory-constrained serving setups. Evaluating directly detecting high-frequency or high-variance patches in latent space would make the method cleaner and more self-contained.

Schedule and hyperparameter tuning per target: The framework relies on several hyperparameters (e.g., transition timesteps e_k, step allocations N_k, stage shifting parameters h_k, and edge patch selection ratio k). While Table S1 details the values determined by numerical optimization, the necessity of re-running JSD minimization and tuning stage divisions for each target model/speedup setting reduces plug-and-play practicality across arbitrary schedules.

Evaluation limited to flow-matching models and lack of video DiTs: The mathematical formulation of NT-DM is tightly coupled with linear rectified flow formulations (FLUX and SD3). As noted in the limitations, standard score-based/DDPM/DDIM models are not evaluated. Furthermore, because spatial/spatiotemporal acceleration is especially vital for video DiTs (e.g., CogVideoX, Open-Sora), demonstrating the method on video generation would substantially reinforce the general impact of the work.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: while most training-free DiT acceleration approaches focus on temporal dimension caching or step skipping, this work investigates spatial acceleration via latent upsampling, which directly yields quadratic reductions in token self-attention complexity.

Solid empirical and theoretical motivation: the paper clearly identifies and dissects the two primary failure modes of latent upsampling—aliasing along semantic boundaries from late upsampling and trajectory mismatch caused by non-isotropic covariance and skewed timestep schedules.

Theoretically principled formulation: the proposed Noise and Timestep Matching (NT-Matching) provides rigorous mathematical derivation for restoring isotropic covariance via correlated noise injection and aligns the effective sampling schedule using analytical/numerical JSD minimization.

Strong experimental validation: extensive benchmarking on FLUX.1-dev and SD3 against multiple state-of-the-art temporal acceleration methods and spatial baselines across quality and alignment metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval), demonstrating orthogonal compatibility with feature forecasting/caching and distilled models.
weaknesses: Under-specified architectural mechanics for mixed-resolution attention: during Stage 2, edge regions are upsampled to full resolution while non-edge regions remain coarse. The manuscript briefly mentions 'matching position embeddings' in Section 4.1, but lacks a detailed explanation of how cross-resolution tokens are structured, indexed, and attended to within the DiT self-attention blocks.

Overhead of intermediate VAE decoding: identifying artifact-prone regions requires Tweedie approximation followed by full VAE decoding and Canny edge detection. While the FLOP overhead is relatively low (~2.48 TFLOPs), executing a full VAE decode mid-inference introduces kernel launches, memory allocation, and CPU-GPU synchronization overhead that can hinder wall-clock latency, especially in batched or latency-critical deployment.

Limited wall-clock latency improvement over simple step reduction: in Table 1, comparing FLUX (10 steps, 5.18s) with RALU (5.04s) or SD3 (14 steps, 2.14s) with RALU (2.04s) reveals relatively modest wall-clock speedup gains compared to the reported theoretical FLOP reductions, likely due to non-uniform token handling and resampling overhead.

Restricted scope to flow-matching formulations: the mathematical derivation of NT-Matching is tailored to linear rectified flow matching schedules and isotropic standard Gaussian noise models, leaving its generalizability to standard variance-preserving/variance-exploding DDPM/DDIM formulations unverified.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: While most DiT acceleration works focus on temporal caching or pruning, training-free spatial acceleration via latent upsampling offers quadratic token reduction and remains relatively unstudied.

Sound diagnosis of failure modes: The paper clearly identifies and separates the two distinct root causes of artifacts in naive latent upsampling—edge-aliasing due to late upsampling and trajectory mismatch caused by non-isotropic noise and skewed timestep distributions.

Principled mathematical formulation: The noise injection parameters (rescaling coefficients and restart timesteps) are derived analytically from flow-matching conditional distributions, and the timestep distribution matching via JSD minimization is well-motivated.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method RALU is evaluated on FLUX-1.dev and SD3 across multiple metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval) and hardware platforms (A100, A6000), consistently outperforming the spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) and remaining competitive with or superior to temporal caching methods at high speedup factors.

Composability: The approach is shown to be orthogonal to and easily combined with both temporal acceleration methods (TaylorSeer, ToCa, Delta-DiT) and distilled models (FLUX.1-schnell, SD3.5L-Turbo), achieving up to 15.9x acceleration with well-preserved visual quality.
weaknesses: Overhead of intermediate VAE decoding: The edge selection process relies on estimating the clean latent via Tweedie's formula and decoding it to pixel space for Canny edge detection. While the FLOP overhead is relatively low (~2.5 TFLOPs), switching back and forth to run the VAE decoder during intermediate diffusion steps adds implementation complexity and potential pipeline latency overheads in real-world deployment.

Clarity on mixed-resolution token handling: The paper describes upsampling the top-r fraction of patches during Stage 2, but details on how the mixed-resolution tokens are arranged, how positional embeddings are indexed for heterogeneous token sizes, and how attention blocks handle this mixed token sequence could be elaborated more explicitly in the main text.

Hyperparameter dependency: The schedule requires choosing stage transition boundaries ($e_k$) and numerically solving for the stage-wise shifting parameters ($h_k$) and noise coefficient ($c$) via JSD optimization for each model/acceleration ratio (as listed in Table S1), meaning it requires some pre-calibration per model configuration.

Scope restricted to flow-matching DiTs: As noted in the limitations, the theoretical derivation of NT-Matching is tailored to rectified flow / flow matching, and its applicability to score-based/DDPM diffusion formulations or non-transformer backbones is not validated.

strengths: Explores an under-investigated and timely problem: While existing training-free DiT acceleration predominantly focuses on temporal caching and step skipping, this work systematically tackles training-free spatial acceleration via latent upsampling.

Clear problem identification and sound mathematical formulation: The paper effectively pinpoints the dual failure modes of naive latent upsampling—high-frequency edge aliasing from late upsampling and trajectory mismatching from noise covariance distortions. The proposed NT-Matching derives closed-form parameters for correlated noise injection and aligns the shifted schedule via JSD minimization.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments on competitive flow-matching DiTs (FLUX.1-dev, SD3, FLUX-schnell, SD3.5L-Turbo) evaluate both visual quality and compositional alignment using a solid suite of metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval).

Orthogonality and composability: The authors convincingly demonstrate that RALU seamlessly composes with existing temporal acceleration techniques (e.g., TaylorSeer, ToCa, Delta-DiT) and step-distilled models, pushing speedups up to 15.9x.

Thorough ablations and qualitative analysis: The submission includes extensive comparisons regarding upsampler selection, edge detection strategies (latent gradient vs. VAE+Canny), adaptive vs. fixed ratios, and uncurated sample grids.
weaknesses: Overhead and pipeline disruption from intermediate VAE decoding: The edge-selection mechanism requires a one-step Tweedie reconstruction followed by a VAE decode to run image-space Canny edge detection. Although FLOP overhead is relatively small (~2.48 TFLOPs), this breaks an otherwise pure latent-space pipeline and may introduce CPU-GPU synchronization or memory transfer overhead in production runtimes.

Architectural mechanism details for mixed-resolution processing: While empirical results are strong, the paper leaves the underlying attention behavior somewhat heuristic (as noted in Section 6). More operational detail regarding how mixed-resolution tokens are embedded (e.g., position embedding / RoPE handling for tokens of differing spatial footprint within the same self-attention layer) in Stage 2 would significantly improve clarity and reproducibility.

Heuristic parameter tuning across stages: The scheduling variables (stage boundaries e, step allocations N, and shifting parameters h, c) appear to require numerical search per model and acceleration target (Table S1). A clearer discussion or automatic heuristic for configuring these parameters without extensive offline search would improve usability.

Scope restricted to Rectified Flow / Flow Matching: The theoretical derivations for NT-Matching are tightly coupled to rectified flow linear interpolation paths. While flow matching is dominant among modern DiTs (FLUX, SD3), its applicability to standard variance-preserving/exploding diffusion formulations remains unexplored.
